6	# SCOP Homology
7	
8	Use the public SCOPe REST API at `https://scop.berkeley.edu/api/v1`.
9	Do not scrape human-facing SCOPe pages or use internal database identifiers.
10	Prefer the release-scoped SCOP MCP tools when they are available; their results
11	include the supporting REST URLs.
12	
13	## Evidence Gates
14	
15	SCOPe facts are data, not facts to reconstruct from model memory.
16	
17	- Do not state a release-specific SID, SUNID, SCCS, hierarchy, boundary,
18	  annotation, periodic label, or numeric value unless it appears in an API
19	  response inspected during the current task.
20	- Do not rank structures by SPACI, AEROSPACI, resolution, R factor, or another
21	  quality measure unless the compared records were retrieved for every
22	  structure. If a required value is absent, do not rank them by that measure.
23	- Do not describe a historical classification change unless the relevant
24	  releases were queried separately or a returned history record supports it.
25	- Do not assert that two domains share a family or superfamily until both
26	  lineages have been retrieved in the same release.
27	- Do not infer a specific substrate, reaction, ligand, phenotype, or
28	  interchangeable structural template from family or superfamily placement
29	  alone.
30	- Do not call domains analogs, convergent, independently evolved, or
31	  nonhomologous merely because SCOPe places them in different superfamilies.
32	  That placement means SCOPe makes no positive homology assertion between
33	  them; it is not proof of a negative evolutionary claim.
34	- Treat BLAST and FATCAT hits for a PDB chain as comparison evidence, not as a
35	  SCOPe assignment. Do not say an unclassified chain or region belongs to a
36	  family, superfamily, or fold solely because it has a retrieved hit.
37	- Do not infer absence of a relationship from an empty or limit-sized hit page.
38	  Verify the requested chain and release, preserve API errors, and report the
39	  bounded search window.
40	
41	If required evidence is unavailable, say that the claim cannot be verified
42	from the available data and name the API request needed. Never fill the gap
43	with a definite answer from memory.
44	
45	## Core Workflow
46	
47	1. Select a stable release for reproducible work.
48	2. Resolve each public identifier or search for the named entity.
49	3. Retrieve the domain or PDB record and its lineage.
50	4. Retrieve annotations and homology warnings before interpreting special
51	   cases.
52	5. Retrieve any additional evidence required by the question, such as quality
53	   records or the same entity in an older release.
54	6. Separate verified SCOPe facts from biological interpretation and from
55	   conclusions SCOPe does not establish.
56	
57	For a request about BLAST or FATCAT matches to one PDB chain, follow the
58	PDB-chain comparison workflow in
59	`references/chain-comparisons.md`. Keep distinct aligned regions separate,
60	check whether the chain already has classified domains, and retrieve lineage
61	and caveat evidence for the representatives that control the interpretation.
62	Inspect `chain.cluster_representative` (metadata) or
63	`subject.cluster_representative` (hits). The API keeps results on the requested
64	chain; when relevant, retrieve the representative explicitly and label its
65	matches as representative evidence. Its local sequence identity and coverage do
66	not transfer its classifications or coordinates to the requested chain. See the
67	cluster section in `references/chain-comparisons.md`.
68	The current FATCAT chain ranges use PDB numbering, while BLAST uses sequence
69	positions. Require a verified mapping before combining their regional evidence.
70	
71	Use only public identifiers:
72	
73	- `sunid`: public numeric identifier for a hierarchy node.
74	- `sid`: public domain identifier.
75	- `sccs`: public class/fold/superfamily/family string.
76	- PDB code.
77	- Public release selector such as `2.08`.
78	
79	Never expose or invent `node_id`, `release_id`, or other internal IDs.
80	
81	## Required Evidence By Claim
82	
83	| Claim | Minimum evidence |
84	|---|---|
85	| Domain identity and boundaries | Domain endpoint in the selected release |
86	| Family, superfamily, fold, or class | Parent lineage in the selected release |
87	| Relationship between two domains | Both lineages in the same release |
88	| Analogy, convergence, independent origin, or absence of homology | Evidence outside hierarchy placement; different superfamilies alone are insufficient |
89	| Artifact, fragment, repeat, or heterogeneity caveat | Annotation and homology responses |
90	| Best structural representative | Quality responses for every candidate |
91	| Historical reclassification | Responses from every compared release |
92	| Current periodic-release status | Current-release metadata |
93	| Specific structural or functional rationale | Retrieved alignment, structure, paper, or other source that states or demonstrates it |
94	| Candidate relationship for a PDB-chain region | Chain metadata, sequence and/or FATCAT hits with aligned ranges, and release-matched lineage and caveats for controlling hit domains |
95	| Historical strong BLAST match | E-value plus the exact target ASTRAL domain-sequence length needed to check N- and C-terminal coverage |
96	| FATCAT-based relationship hypothesis | FATCAT P-value, score, initial RMSD, competing lineages, and representative-set provenance when available; verified residue mapping and inspected alignment/structure for regional agreement, paired coverage, or topology claims |
97	
98	Use `scripts/scop_compare.py` for deterministic domain-lineage and quality
99	comparisons when local execution and network access are available. The script
100	fails rather than inventing a comparison when required records are missing.
101	
102	## Biological Interpretation
103	
104	- The domain is the fundamental classified unit. A chain can contain multiple,
105	  inserted, discontinuous, swapped, or intertwined domains.
106	- A shared family normally indicates the closer SCOPe relationship.
107	- A shared superfamily supports probable common ancestry, but not exact
108	  biochemical function.
109	- A shared fold or class indicates structural similarity. It does not by itself
110	  establish common ancestry.
111	- Agreement between BLAST and FATCAT evidence over the same chain region can
112	  strengthen a non-official relationship hypothesis, but it does not create an
113	  official classification. A FATCAT match alone establishes structural
114	  similarity, not homology.
115	- Protein structure is often conserved after sequence similarity has fallen
116	  below BLAST detection. Therefore, an extensive FATCAT match can be the most
117	  informative evidence for a remote-homology hypothesis when no qualifying
118	  sequence hit is returned. Treat it as a structure-led candidate: examine
119	  topology, alignment extent, competing superfamilies, and caveats before
120	  proposing homology, and stop at fold-level similarity when superfamily-level
121	  ancestry is not discriminated. Current chain-hit summaries do not expose
122	  residue correspondence or topology; without that evidence, report structural
123	  candidates and the unresolved checks.
124	- Different superfamilies within a fold mean that SCOPe does not assert common
125	  ancestry at the superfamily level. Say exactly that. Do not strengthen it to
126	  "unrelated," "analogous," or "convergent" without independent evidence.
127	- Protein and species levels are SCOPe hierarchy levels and must not be treated
128	  as equivalent to external taxonomy or sequence-database records.
129	- An automated match is not automatically low quality, but it should be
130	  reported as automated when that status matters.
131	- SPACI and AEROSPACI measure structural quality for representative selection;
132	  they are not homology or functional-similarity scores.
133	- Stable releases are the normal basis for reproducible analysis. Periodic
134	  updates do not replace stable releases.
135	
136	For detailed hierarchy semantics, special annotations, and biological
137	limitations, read `references/biological-interpretation.md`.
138	
139	## API Navigation
140	
141	- Exact identifier: use the corresponding `sids`, `sunids`, or `sccs`
142	  release-scoped endpoint.
143	- Unknown identifier type: use `/releases/{release}/resolve/{identifier}`.
144	- Name or keyword: use `/releases/{release}/search?q=...` with a small limit,
145	  then resolve the selected result.
146	- Lineage: use `/parents`.
147	- Descendants: use `/children?limit=...` and follow opaque cursors.
148	- PDB domains: use `/releases/{release}/pdb/{code}/domains`.
149	- PDB chain and its existing classifications: use
150	  `/releases/{release}/chains/{chain}`.
151	- Combined BLAST and FATCAT chain comparisons: use
152	  `/releases/{release}/chains/{chain}/hits?limit=...`.
153	- One comparison stream only: use `/sequence-hits` or `/structure-hits` below
154	  that chain path.
155	- Caveats: use `/annotations` and `/homology`.
156	- Quality: use `/releases/{release}/pdb/{code}/quality`.
157	- Current release: use `/releases/current`.
158	
159	Read `references/api-usage.md` for exact endpoint patterns and pagination. Read
160	`references/chain-comparisons.md` before deciding whether chain-comparison
161	evidence supports a regional family, superfamily, or fold hypothesis.
162	
163	## Answer Discipline
164	
165	Structure a biological answer around:
166	
167	1. **Verified SCOPe facts:** release, public identifiers, hierarchy, and
168	   annotations actually retrieved.
169	2. **Interpretation:** the relationship justified by the deepest shared
170	   homology-bearing level and any structural evidence actually inspected.
171	3. **Limits:** functions, mechanisms, histories, or rankings not established by
172	   the retrieved data.
173	4. **Evidence:** concise release-scoped API paths used.
174	
175	For a PDB-chain comparison, first state whether SCOPe already classifies any
176	domains on the chain. Then report each material chain region separately, with
177	the sequence and structure streams, alignment ranges, metrics, retrieved
178	lineages, conflicts, and search-window limits. Name the coordinate system and
179	leave cross-stream overlap unresolved when a residue mapping is unavailable.
180	Label any proposed relationship as non-official and distinguish it from curated
181	domain boundaries.
182

184	name, shared ligand, motif, fold, or quality score into a stronger evolutionary
185	claim than the hierarchy supports. If a question asks *why* a classification

name: scop-homology
description: Use classic SCOP, ASTRAL, and SCOPe structural-classification data through public SCOPe API tools to answer questions about protein domains, hierarchy, homology, folds, families, superfamilies, PDB-chain BLAST and FATCAT comparisons, stable releases, ASTRAL quality, and reproducible citations. Use for SCOP/SCOPe/ASTRAL questions only; this skill does not cover SCOP2, CATH, ECOD, or other classification resources.
---

# SCOP Homology

Use the public SCOPe REST API at `https://scop.berkeley.edu/api/v1`.
Do not scrape human-facing SCOPe pages or use internal database identifiers.
Prefer the release-scoped SCOP MCP tools when they are available; their results
include the supporting REST URLs.

## Evidence Gates

SCOPe facts are data, not facts to reconstruct from model memory.

- Do not state a release-specific SID, SUNID, SCCS, hierarchy, boundary,
  annotation, periodic label, or numeric value unless it appears in an API
  response inspected during the current task.
- Do not rank structures by SPACI, AEROSPACI, resolution, R factor, or another
  quality measure unless the compared records were retrieved for every
  structure. If a required value is absent, do not rank them by that measure.
- Do not describe a historical classification change unless the relevant
  releases were queried separately or a returned history record supports it.
- Do not assert that two domains share a family or superfamily until both
  lineages have been retrieved in the same release.
- Do not infer a specific substrate, reaction, ligand, phenotype, or
  interchangeable structural template from family or superfamily placement
  alone.
- Do not call domains analogs, convergent, independently evolved, or
  nonhomologous merely because SCOPe places them in different superfamilies.
  That placement means SCOPe makes no positive homology assertion between
  them; it is not proof of a negative evolutionary claim.
- Treat BLAST and FATCAT hits for a PDB chain as comparison evidence, not as a
  SCOPe assignment. Do not say an unclassified chain or region belongs to a
  family, superfamily, or fold solely because it has a retrieved hit.
- Do not infer absence of a relationship from an empty or limit-sized hit page.
  Verify the requested chain and release, preserve API errors, and report the
  bounded search window.

If required evidence is unavailable, say that the claim cannot be verified
from the available data and name the API request needed. Never fill the gap
with a definite answer from memory.

## Core Workflow

1. Select a stable release for reproducible work.
2. Resolve each public identifier or search for the named entity.
3. Retrieve the domain or PDB record and its lineage.
4. Retrieve annotations and homology warnings before interpreting special
   cases.
5. Retrieve any additional evidence required by the question, such as quality
   records or the same entity in an older release.
6. Separate verified SCOPe facts from biological interpretation and from
   conclusions SCOPe does not establish.

For a request about BLAST or FATCAT matches to one PDB chain, follow the
PDB-chain comparison workflow in
`references/chain-comparisons.md`. Keep distinct aligned regions separate,
check whether the chain already has classified domains, and retrieve lineage
and caveat evidence for the representatives that control the interpretation.
Inspect `chain.cluster_representative` (metadata) or
`subject.cluster_representative` (hits). The API keeps results on the requested
chain; when relevant, retrieve the representative explicitly and label its
matches as representative evidence. Its local sequence identity and coverage do
not transfer its classifications or coordinates to the requested chain. See the
cluster section in `references/chain-comparisons.md`.
The current FATCAT chain ranges use PDB numbering, while BLAST uses sequence
positions. Require a verified mapping before combining their regional evidence.

Use only public identifiers:

- `sunid`: public numeric identifier for a hierarchy node.
- `sid`: public domain identifier.
- `sccs`: public class/fold/superfamily/family string.
- PDB code.
- Public release selector such as `2.08`.

Never expose or invent `node_id`, `release_id`, or other internal IDs.

## Required Evidence By Claim

| Claim | Minimum evidence |
|---|---|
| Domain identity and boundaries | Domain endpoint in the selected release |
| Family, superfamily, fold, or class | Parent lineage in the selected release |
| Relationship between two domains | Both lineages in the same release |
| Analogy, convergence, independent origin, or absence of homology | Evidence outside hierarchy placement; different superfamilies alone are insufficient |
| Artifact, fragment, repeat, or heterogeneity caveat | Annotation and homology responses |
| Best structural representative | Quality responses for every candidate |
| Historical reclassification | Responses from every compared release |
| Current periodic-release status | Current-release metadata |
| Specific structural or functional rationale | Retrieved alignment, structure, paper, or other source that states or demonstrates it |
| Candidate relationship for a PDB-chain region | Chain metadata, sequence and/or FATCAT hits with aligned ranges, and release-matched lineage and caveats for controlling hit domains |
| Historical strong BLAST match | E-value plus the exact target ASTRAL domain-sequence length needed to check N- and C-terminal coverage |
| FATCAT-based relationship hypothesis | FATCAT P-value, score, initial RMSD, competing lineages, and representative-set provenance when available; verified residue mapping and inspected alignment/structure for regional agreement, paired coverage, or topology claims |

Use `scripts/scop_compare.py` for deterministic domain-lineage and quality
comparisons when local execution and network access are available. The script
fails rather than inventing a comparison when required records are missing.

## Biological Interpretation

- The domain is the fundamental classified unit. A chain can contain multiple,
  inserted, discontinuous, swapped, or intertwined domains.
- A shared family normally indicates the closer SCOPe relationship.
- A shared superfamily supports probable common ancestry, but not exact
  biochemical function.
- A shared fold or class indicates structural similarity. It does not by itself
  establish common ancestry.
- Agreement between BLAST and FATCAT evidence over the same chain region can
  strengthen a non-official relationship hypothesis, but it does not create an
  official classification. A FATCAT match alone establishes structural
  similarity, not homology.
- Protein structure is often conserved after sequence similarity has fallen
  below BLAST detection. Therefore, an extensive FATCAT match can be the most
  informative evidence for a remote-homology hypothesis when no qualifying
  sequence hit is returned. Treat it as a structure-led candidate: examine
  topology, alignment extent, competing superfamilies, and caveats before
  proposing homology, and stop at fold-level similarity when superfamily-level
  ancestry is not discriminated. Current chain-hit summaries do not expose
  residue correspondence or topology; without that evidence, report structural
  candidates and the unresolved checks.
- Different superfamilies within a fold mean that SCOPe does not assert common
  ancestry at the superfamily level. Say exactly that. Do not strengthen it to
  "unrelated," "analogous," or "convergent" without independent evidence.
- Protein and species levels are SCOPe hierarchy levels and must not be treated
  as equivalent to external taxonomy or sequence-database records.
- An automated match is not automatically low quality, but it should be
  reported as automated when that status matters.
- SPACI and AEROSPACI measure structural quality for representative selection;
  they are not homology or functional-similarity scores.
- Stable releases are the normal basis for reproducible analysis. Periodic
  updates do not replace stable releases.

For detailed hierarchy semantics, special annotations, and biological
limitations, read `references/biological-interpretation.md`.

## API Navigation

- Exact identifier: use the corresponding `sids`, `sunids`, or `sccs`
  release-scoped endpoint.
- Unknown identifier type: use `/releases/{release}/resolve/{identifier}`.
- Name or keyword: use `/releases/{release}/search?q=...` with a small limit,
  then resolve the selected result.
- Lineage: use `/parents`.
- Descendants: use `/children?limit=...` and follow opaque cursors.
- PDB domains: use `/releases/{release}/pdb/{code}/domains`.
- PDB chain and its existing classifications: use
  `/releases/{release}/chains/{chain}`.
- Combined BLAST and FATCAT chain comparisons: use
  `/releases/{release}/chains/{chain}/hits?limit=...`.
- One comparison stream only: use `/sequence-hits` or `/structure-hits` below
  that chain path.
- Caveats: use `/annotations` and `/homology`.
- Quality: use `/releases/{release}/pdb/{code}/quality`.
- Current release: use `/releases/current`.

Read `references/api-usage.md` for exact endpoint patterns and pagination. Read
`references/chain-comparisons.md` before deciding whether chain-comparison
evidence supports a regional family, superfamily, or fold hypothesis.

## Answer Discipline

Structure a biological answer around:

1. **Verified SCOPe facts:** release, public identifiers, hierarchy, and
   annotations actually retrieved.
2. **Interpretation:** the relationship justified by the deepest shared
   homology-bearing level and any structural evidence actually inspected.
3. **Limits:** functions, mechanisms, histories, or rankings not established by
   the retrieved data.
4. **Evidence:** concise release-scoped API paths used.

For a PDB-chain comparison, first state whether SCOPe already classifies any
domains on the chain. Then report each material chain region separately, with
the sequence and structure streams, alignment ranges, metrics, retrieved
lineages, conflicts, and search-window limits. Name the coordinate system and
leave cross-stream overlap unresolved when a residue mapping is unavailable.
Label any proposed relationship as non-official and distinguish it from curated
domain boundaries.

Do not turn absence of a warning into positive evidence. Do not turn a protein
name, shared ligand, motif, fold, or quality score into a stronger evolutionary
claim than the hierarchy supports. If a question asks *why* a classification
changed but the available API only shows that it changed, report the
classification change and state that its sequence, structural, or literature
rationale was not verified from the available evidence.

1	# Biological Interpretation With SCOP And SCOPe
2	
3	Use this reference after retrieving the relevant SCOPe API records. It explains
4	what the hierarchy can support; it is not a substitute for release-specific
5	data.
6	
7	## Hierarchy Semantics

# Biological Interpretation With SCOP And SCOPe

Use this reference after retrieving the relevant SCOPe API records. It explains
what the hierarchy can support; it is not a substitute for release-specific
data.

## Hierarchy Semantics

SCOP/SCOPe is domain-centered. A PDB chain can contain one domain, multiple
domains, an inserted domain, noncontiguous domains, swapped elements, tags, or
regions outside ordinary globular classes.

- `class`: broad secondary-structure organization.
- `fold`: similar major secondary structures in the same arrangement and
  topology.
- `superfamily`: families inferred to share common evolutionary origin from
  structural, functional, and sequence evidence.
- `family`: a closer relationship, usually supported by sequence similarity or
  very similar function and structure.
- `protein`: essentially the same function across species or isoforms.
- `species`: a distinct sequence and its variants in SCOPe terminology.
- `domain`: a classified structural instance with a SID and SUNID.

Family and superfamily are homology-bearing levels. Fold and class alone are
structural categories, not positive SCOPe assertions of common ancestry.

## Relationship Decisions

For two domains:

1. Retrieve both lineages in the same release.
2. Identify the deepest shared class, fold, superfamily, and family nodes.
3. Check annotations and homology warnings for both domains.
4. State only the relationship justified by the evidence:
   - shared family: close SCOPe relationship;
   - shared superfamily but different families: probable common ancestry;
   - shared fold but different superfamilies: structural/topological
     similarity, not a SCOPe homology assertion;
   - shared class only: broad architectural similarity.

Do not infer a specific reaction, substrate, ligand, pathway role, phenotype,
oligomeric state, or interchangeable template from a superfamily assignment.
Those conclusions require additional sequence, active-site, ligand,
domain-architecture, genomic-context, or experimental evidence.

Different superfamilies are also not a positive SCOPe assertion of analogy,
convergence, independent origin, or absence of homology. Use the asymmetric
statement: SCOPe supports shared fold-level structure but does not assert
superfamily-level common ancestry. A stronger positive or negative
evolutionary conclusion needs independent evidence.

When explaining a proposed remote relationship, distinguish evidence that was
actually inspected from evidence that would be needed. Relevant evidence can
include a global structural alignment and matching topology, sequence
correspondence at equivalent core positions, conserved motifs in equivalent
structural contexts, compatible domain architecture and biological context,
phylogenetic support, and experiments. Do not list these as observations
unless the source or result was retrieved.

## Domain Boundaries And Modularity

A domain need not be contiguous in sequence. Insertions and rearrangements can
place one evolutionary module inside another. Compare domains rather than whole
chains so unrelated inserts, tags, or adjacent domains do not create false
similarity or obscure a real relationship.

Historical boundary changes can reflect newly observed evolutionary contexts.
Do not describe a particular change unless every compared release was queried.

## Special Annotations

Machine-readable heterogeneity annotations can qualify ordinary hierarchy
interpretation:

- `md`: multiple alternative domain divisions.
- `re`: repeat-based domains with different repeat counts.
- `fr`: fragment.
- `as`: additional subdomains.
- `ie`: additional insertions or extensions.
- `ms`: missing secondary structures.
- `ae`: additional elements.
- `me`: missing elements.
- `nf`: not a true fold.
- `hf`: heterogeneous fold.
- `dn`: different domains contain different subsets of subdomains.

Artifacts, synthetic tags, fragments, repeats, heterogeneous families, and
"not true" groupings should not be used as ordinary homology or benchmark
examples without preserving the caveat.

Annotations constrain an interpretation; they do not automatically erase a
family or superfamily relationship. Explain exactly which inference is
affected.

## Representative Selection

ASTRAL subsets reduce sequence redundancy. SPACI and AEROSPACI support
technical-quality comparisons and representative selection. They are not
evolutionary or functional scores.

Retrieve quality records for every candidate. Compare actual values together
with method, resolution, R factor, and available validation fields. A
technically preferred representative does not replace alternative ligand,
conformational, oligomeric, or biological states.

Never rank candidates when the requested quality measure is unavailable for
one or more of them.

## Dataset Design

For remote-homology benchmarks:

- Separate training and test examples by family while keeping positives within
  a verified superfamily.
- Use same-fold, different-superfamily examples only as labeled operational
  `SCOPe-negative` pairs, meaning no SCOPe superfamily-level homology assertion.
  They are not proven biological nonhomologs. Preserve annotations and run
  sensitivity analyses because future evidence or curation can reveal remote
  relationships.
- Remove sequence leakage with an appropriate ASTRAL nonredundant subset.
- Preserve biologically meaningful diversity rather than selecting only the
  single highest-quality structure.
- Exclude or stratify artifacts, fragments, repeats, and heterogeneous
  groupings.
- Freeze the SCOPe release, selection rules, thresholds, and representative
  choices.

## Automated Classification

SCOPe combines manual curation with validated automated classification.
Automation is useful for placing new structures into established regions of
the hierarchy. Manual curation remains important for new folds and
superfamilies, remote relationships, artifacts, boundary corrections,
heterogeneity, and large complexes.

Do not equate automated classification with low quality. Report automated
status when it affects provenance or interpretation.

## Epistemic Boundaries

Separate four kinds of statement:

1. **Retrieved fact:** directly present in a cited API response.
2. **SCOPe interpretation:** follows from the retrieved hierarchy and
   annotation semantics.
3. **Biological hypothesis:** plausible but requires evidence outside SCOPe.
4. **Unknown from available data:** cannot be determined because a necessary
   record was not retrieved or the API does not expose it.

Use qualified language for hypotheses. Use explicit abstention for unknown
release-specific facts. Do not convert uncertainty into a confident database
claim. In particular, a retrieved classification change does not by itself
retrieve the structural, sequence, or functional rationale for that change.

content.text:
## What I found

I verified the reclassification in both releases and gathered the supporting structural evidence.

**The change.** In SCOPe 2.04 the two domains shared nothing below class. In current SCOPe (2.08) they share a superfamily. The ColG domain moved; the Cry3A domain did not.

| Domain | SCOPe 2.04 | SCOPe 2.08 |
|---|---|---|
| ColG, 1nqd chain A | b.23.2.1 | b.18.1.36 |
| Cry3A C-terminal, 1dlc A:500-644 | b.18.1.3 | b.18.1.3 |

The deterministic comparison returned `same_class` in 2.04 and `same_superfamily` in 2.08.

**Evidence for common ancestry.** Three independent strands, all retrieved:

- The curated family annotation on b.18.1.36 cites PubMed 17977833 as describing likely homology between a ColG collagen-binding domain, the Cry4Ba C-terminal domain d1w99a3, and the enterotoxin C-terminal domain d2quoa_. The Cry4Ba domain sits in b.18.1.3, the same family as the Cry3A domain.
- Structural alignment links both sides to shared third-party members of b.18.1. The ColG representative 1nqjA matches d1w99a3 at P 0.00395 and 2.52 Å, and 1dlcA matches the same domain at P 0.0002 and 1.43 Å.
- Both chains independently match the xylanase D domain d1ux7a_ in family b.18.1.28.

In 2.04, the ColG collagen-binding domain d1nqda_ (sunid 86025, '1nqd A:') was classified b.23.2.1: class b (All beta proteins, sunid 48724), fold b.23 CUB-like (49853), superfamily b.23.2 Collagen-binding domain (89260), family b.23.2.1 Collagen-binding domain (89261), protein Class 1 collagenase (89262), species Clostridium histolyticum [TaxId 1498] (89263). In the same release, the Cry3A C-terminal domain d1dlca1 (sunid 23719, '1dlc A:500-644') was classified b.18.1.3: fold b.18 Galactose-binding domain-like (49784), superfamily b.18.1 Galactose-binding domain-like (49785), family b.18.1.3 delta-Endotoxin, C-terminal domain (49796), species Bacillus thuringiensis tenebrionis, CRYIIIA (BT13) [TaxId 1444] (49798). The deterministic two-domain comparison in 2.04 returned relationship 'same_class' with lowest shared node = class b (48724): different folds, different superfamilies, no SCOPe homology assertion of any kind between them.

In 2.08, d1nqda_ (same sunid 86025) is classified b.18.1.36: fold b.18 Galactose-binding domain-like (49784), superfamily b.18.1 Galactose-binding domain-like (49785), family b.18.1.36 Collagen-binding domain (new node, sunid 267607), protein Class 1 collagenase (267633), species Clostridium histolyticum [TaxId 1498] (267693). d1dlca1 is unchanged in 2.08: still b.18.1.3 under superfamily 49785 with the same sunids. The 2.08 comparison returns relationship 'same_superfamily' with lowest shared node = superfamily b.18.1 Galactose-binding domain-like (sunid 49785), interpreted by the service as 'consistent with probable common ancestry'.

So the correct evolutionary strength changed by exactly one homology-bearing level: 2.04 asserted nothing (shared class only, a broad architectural category), while 2.08 places both domains in one superfamily but in different families (b.18.1.36 for ColG versus b.18.1.3 for Cry3A). Superfamily sharing supports probable common ancestry; it is not a family-level relationship and does not imply close sequence kinship or equivalent biochemistry.

NODE-LEVEL BOOKKEEPING OF THE MOVE

The move was a reclassification into an existing superfamily, not a merger of two superfamilies. The old ColG superfamily node b.23.2 (sunid 89260) returns HTTP 404 in 2.08: it no longer exists. The receiving family node b.18.1.36 (sunid 267607) returns HTTP 404 in 2.04: it is new. The old fold b.23 CUB-like (sunid 49853) still exists in 2.08, but ColG is no longer in it. The target superfamily b.18.1 (49785) has the same sunid in both releases, so ColG was relocated into the long-standing Galactose-binding domain-like superfamily that already contained the delta-endotoxin C-terminal family.

A related boundary and domain-count change occurred on 1nqd chain B. In 2.04, chain B held a single whole-chain domain (sunid 86026, '1nqd B:', b.23.2.1). In 2.08, chain B holds d1nqdb1 (sunid 86026, 'B:893-1008', b.18.1.36) plus d1nqdb2 (sunid 281794, 'B:891-892', l.1.1.1, whose SCCS resolves to the Synthetic species node under the artifacts class). Chain A remains a single whole-chain domain, d1nqda_. 1dlc is unchanged across the two releases and retains three domains: d1dlca1 (b.18.1.3, A:500-644), d1dlca2 (b.77.2.1, A:290-499), and d1dlca3 (f.1.3.1, A:61-289).

STRUCTURAL AND FUNCTIONAL EVIDENCE SUPPORTING COMMON ANCESTRY

1. Curated literature rationale recorded on the receiving family. The 2.08 annotations for family b.18.1.36 (sunid 267607) carry the comment 'PubMed 17977833 describes likely homology between (linkscop: d2quoa_), (linkscop: d1w99a3), and (linkscop: d1nqdb_)', with PubMed 17977833 as a structured xref. This is the single most direct piece of retrieved rationale, because the cited partners bracket exactly the relationship asked about: d1w99a3 (1w99 A:472-641) is classified b.18.1.3 delta-Endotoxin, C-terminal domain, Bacillus thuringiensis Cry4Ba, i.e. the same family as the Cry3A domain d1dlca1; and d2quoa_ (2quo A:) is b.18.1.37 Clostridium perfringens enterotoxin (CPE), C-terminal domain. The annotation therefore ties the ColG collagen-binding module to the delta-endotoxin C-terminal family through a published analysis, and the enterotoxin C-terminal domain supplies an intermediate that makes the ColG-to-delta-endotoxin link a chain of related beta-sandwich modules rather than an isolated pairwise guess. Two caveats: I retrieved the annotation record, not the publication, so the paper's actual arguments, alignments, and figures were not inspected; and the comment names the SID d1nqdb_, which is the 2.04-era whole-chain-B identifier, whereas 2.08 splits chain B into d1nqdb1 and d1nqdb2.

2. Structural-alignment evidence triangulated through shared superfamily members. 1nqdA itself has no stored FATCAT structure hits; its stream is empty because it is not a representative. Its cluster_representative is 1nqjA (not the requested chain), related by Smith-Waterman local alignment at 99.16 percent identity over 119 alignment columns, member coverage 97.54 percent, representative coverage 100 percent. Treating 1nqjA's matches explicitly as representative evidence, its FATCAT stream contains a graded ladder within superfamily b.18.1: strongest to its own family b.18.1.36 (d5ikua1, 5iku A:773-890, P = 4.2e-14, score 231.63, initial RMSD 1.72 A, 28.71 percent identity); then to the enterotoxin C-terminal family b.18.1.37 (d2quoa_, P = 1.4e-6, score 151.55, initial RMSD 2.49 A, 10.26 percent identity); and then, weakly but within the filter, to the delta-endotoxin C-terminal family b.18.1.3 (d1w99a3, P = 0.00395, score 94.24, initial RMSD 2.52 A, 2.5 percent identity, 12.5 percent similarity, 94 chain-side residues from author residue 911 against 160 domain-side residues from 472). In the reverse direction, 1dlcA is its own representative, and its FATCAT stream matches the same Cry4Ba C-terminal domain d1w99a3 much more strongly (P = 0.0002, score 282.5, initial RMSD 1.43 A, 25.77 percent identity, 144 chain-side residues from author residue 501 against 163 domain-side residues from 472), consistent with d1w99a3 being a same-family relative of d1dlca1. Both sides also independently reach a common third-party member of the superfamily: the xylanase D domain d1ux7a_ in family b.18.1.28 (from 1nqjA, P = 0.00132, score 94.19, initial RMSD 3.80 A; from 1dlcA, P = 0.00746, score 203.97, initial RMSD 2.37 A). 1dlcA additionally reaches d1w9wa_ (b.18.1.10, P = 0.0076, initial RMSD 1.58 A) and d2qkga3 (b.18.1.0, P = 2.98e-5). This pattern, in which each domain aligns to multiple distinct families of b.18.1 at modest RMSD over most of a roughly 90 to 145 residue beta-sandwich, is the kind of extensive, mutually corroborating structural signal that supports a superfamily-level grouping; it is also the pattern the skill flags as the most informative evidence class for remote homology when sequence similarity has decayed.

3. Absence of sequence support, which is itself diagnostic of remoteness rather than of non-relationship. The complete BLAST stream for 1nqjA (page exhausted, has_more false, filter maximum log10 E-value -1, rejected sequences excluded) contains only b.18.1.36 collagen-binding domains (d5ikua2 at log10 E -61.9 and 98.73 percent identity; d1nqjb_ at log10 E -60.9), b.18.1.0 automated matches in the same region (d5sv5a_ at log10 E -16.9, 36.61 percent identity; several 3jqw and 3jqx domains near log10 E -9.2), and marginal immunoglobulin-like b.1.1.0 hits at about 14.5 percent identity and log10 E near -1.76. No delta-endotoxin C-terminal domain and no b.18.1.3 domain appears anywhere in that stream. The 1dlcA BLAST stream (has_more true, so bounded) returns only its own chain's domains and close Cry relatives, topped by d1dlca3 (f.1.3.1, log10 E -134.9), d1dlca2 (b.77.2.1, log10 E -123.3), d1ji6a3 and d1ji6a2 from Cry3Bb1, and d1dlca1 itself (log10 E -80.1, chain positions 440-584 against domain positions 1-145). Sequence evidence therefore does not support the ColG-to-Cry3A link at all; the relationship is below BLAST detection, which is exactly why it needed structural and curatorial evidence and why it moved only at superfamily rather than family level.

4. Functional and architectural compatibility, stated as interpretation rather than as a retrieved mechanism. Both modules are accessory, non-catalytic beta-sandwich units appended to the end of a larger secreted bacterial multidomain protein. The 1nqd entry is described as the ColG collagenase collagen-binding domain 3b at 1.65 A in the presence of calcium, with keywords beta sandwich, metalloprotease, collagen-binding domain, calcium, hydrolase, and the domain record for d1nqda_ carries the comment 'complexed with ca' in both 2.04 and 2.08. Its chain record lists gene ColG and UniProt Q9S0X0. The 1dlc domain d1dlca1 is the C-terminal module of a three-domain chain whose other two modules are classified in unrelated parts of the hierarchy (b.77.2.1 and f.1.3.1), so the b.18.1 module is a discrete appended unit there as well. The receiving superfamily is named Galactose-binding domain-like, and its families include carbohydrate-active enzyme accessory modules such as b.18.1.28 endo-1,4-beta-xylanase D and b.18.1.25 rhamnogalacturonase B C-terminal domain, plus protease C-terminal modules such as b.18.1.20 (alkaline serine protease KP-43 and kexin C-terminal domains). A shared role as a ligand- or surface-binding ancillary module on secreted bacterial proteins is thus consistent with the superfamily placement. This is compatible context, not proof; I did not retrieve binding assays, mutagenesis, or active-site comparisons.

LIMITS THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THIS ANSWER

Homology strength. Shared superfamily b.18.1 in 2.08 supports probable common ancestry only. The two domains are in different families (b.18.1.36 versus b.18.1.3), so SCOPe makes no closer assertion. Equally, the 2.04 state must not be described as evidence of analogy, convergence, or non-homology; different superfamilies in 2.04 meant only that SCOPe made no positive homology assertion then, and the 2.08 reclassification shows how such a placement can change.

Function transfer. Collagen binding, calcium binding, the hydrolase context of ColG, and the activity of the Cry3A protein must not be transferred across the superfamily in either direction. A shared superfamily does not establish a shared substrate, ligand, metal requirement, oligomeric state, pathway role, or phenotype. The b.18.1 superfamily is explicitly heterogeneous in function, spanning xylanase, rhamnogalacturonase, protease, and other accessory modules.

The usable structural signal between the ColG side and the delta-endotoxin C-terminal family is weak (P = 0.00395, 2.5 percent identity, initial RMSD 2.52 A over about 94 aligned residues), which is adequate as superfamily-level evidence but not adequate for comparative modelling, for mapping functional residues, or for inferring an equivalent binding site.

I did not retrieve SPACI or AEROSPACI values for either entry, so I rank neither structure by quality.

Coordinate systems and unresolved mapping. FATCAT chain and domain ranges above are in PDB author residue numbering and are reported as per-side residue counts with open-ended ends, whereas BLAST ranges are one-based sequence positions. The cluster-representative similarity ranges are one-based positions in seqres-minus-tags and are not a residue-by-residue mapping. I did not obtain a verified residue mapping, so I do not merge the sequence and structure ranges, and I make no claim about residue correspondence, topology equivalence, or precise boundary agreement between the ColG and Cry3A modules.

Search-window bounds, and what they do and do not show. No direct FATCAT pair between 1nqd and 1dlc was returned in either direction. The 1dlcA structure stream was exhausted under its filters (has_more false, limit 40, P at most 0.05, initial RMSD under 4 A) and contained no b.18.1.36 collagen-binding domain; the 1nqjA structure stream was not exhausted (has_more true at limit 40). Under the skill's rules this bounded, filtered absence is not evidence against the relationship; the official 2.08 superfamily placement, not any hit list, is what establishes the shared level. Several supporting hits and several b.18.1.0 domains are automated matches, which I report as automated provenance rather than as a quality judgement.

Caveat status. The homology and annotation records show no heterogeneity codes and no warnings for d1nqda_ or d1dlca1 in either release; caveats_present was false in both comparisons. Superfamily b.18.1 reports homology_scope sf with no warnings, and family b.18.1.36 reports homology_scope fa with no warnings. Per the skill, I do not convert that absence of warnings into extra positive evidence. Family b.18.1.3 is mapped to Pfam PF03944 by an automatic mapping comment; family b.18.1.36 carries no Pfam xref, so no cross-database family equivalence is claimed.

Rationale for the change itself. The retrieved records establish what changed and preserve the curated pointer to PubMed 17977833 as the recorded reason, but I did not read that publication, and the API returned no explicit change-history record describing the reclassification. The detailed sequence, structural, and functional argument that drove curators to dissolve superfamily b.23.2 and create family b.18.1.36 under b.18.1 is therefore reported as cited but not A shared role as a ligand- or surface-binding ancillary module on secreted bacterial proteins is thus consistent with the superfamily placement. This is compatible context, not proof; I did not retrieve binding assays, mutagenesis, or active-site comparisons.

LIMITS THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THIS ANSWER

Homology strength. Shared superfamily b.18.1 in 2.08 supports probable common ancestry only. The two domains are in different families (b.18.1.36 versus b.18.1.3), so SCOPe makes no closer assertion. Equally, the 2.04 state must not be described as evidence of analogy, convergence, or non-homology; different superfamilies in 2.04 meant only that SCOPe made no positive homology assertion then, and the 2.08 reclassification shows how such a placement can change.

Function transfer. Collagen binding, calcium binding, the hydrolase context of ColG, and the activity of the Cry3A protein must not be transferred across the superfamily in either direction. A shared superfamily does not establish a shared substrate, ligand, metal requirement, oligomeric state, pathway role, or phenotype. The b.18.1 superfamily is explicitly heterogeneous in function, spanning xylanase, rhamnogalacturonase, protease, and other accessory modules.

Template and structure-transfer use. Neither domain is a validated modelling template for the other. The usable structural signal between the ColG side and the delta-endotoxin C-terminal family is weak (P = 0.00395, 2.5 percent identity, initial RMSD 2.52 A over about 94 aligned residues), which is adequate as superfamily-level evidence but not adequate for comparative modelling, for mapping functional residues, or for inferring an equivalent binding site.

Representative selection. The requested chain 1nqdA has no stored FATCAT hits. Everything in strand 2 on the ColG side comes from 1nqjA, a different chain and the 90-percent-identity cluster representative. Its matches, coordinates, and any classification must not be attributed directly to 1nqdA, even at 99.16 percent local identity; only the official record for d1nqda_ classifies that chain. I did not retrieve SPACI or AEROSPACI values for either entry, so I rank neither structure by quality.

Coordinate systems and unresolved mapping. FATCAT chain and domain ranges above are in PDB author residue numbering and are reported as per-side residue counts with open-ended ends, whereas BLAST ranges are one-based sequence positions. The cluster-representative similarity ranges are one-based positions in seqres-minus-tags and are not a residue-by-residue mapping. I did not obtain a verified residue mapping, so I do not merge the sequence and structure ranges, and I make no claim about residue correspondence, topology equivalence, or precise boundary agreement between the ColG and Cry3A modules.

Search-window bounds, and what they do and do not show. No direct FATCAT pair between 1nqd and 1dlc was returned in either direction. The 1dlcA structure stream was exhausted under its filters (has_more false, limit 40, P at most 0.05, initial RMSD under 4 A) and contained no b.18.1.36 collagen-binding domain; the 1nqjA structure stream was not exhausted (has_more true at limit 40). Under the skill's rules this bounded, filtered absence is not evidence against the relationship; the official 2.08 superfamily placement, not any hit list, is what establishes the shared level. Several supporting hits and several b.18.1.0 domains are automated matches, which I report as automated provenance rather than as a quality judgement.

Caveat status. The homology and annotation records show no heterogeneity codes and no warnings for d1nqda_ or d1dlca1 in either release; caveats_present was false in both comparisons. Superfamily b.18.1 reports homology_scope sf with no warnings, and family b.18.1.36 reports homology_scope fa with no warnings. Per the skill, I do not convert that absence of warnings into extra positive evidence. Family b.18.1.3 is mapped to Pfam PF03944 by an automatic mapping comment; family b.18.1.36 carries no Pfam xref, so no cross-database family equivalence is claimed.

Rationale for the change itself. The retrieved records establish what changed and preserve the curated pointer to PubMed 17977833 as the recorded reason, but I did not read that publication, and the API returned no explicit change-history record describing the reclassification. The detailed sequence, structural, and functional argument that drove curators to dissolve superfamily b.23.2 and create family b.18.1.36 under b.18.1 is therefore reported as cited but not independently verified from the evidence I inspected.
